summary:
ASTRONAUT MISSION TRAINER is a pixel-art mobile game that turns kids aged 7 to 12 into the commander of a base on Mars. Players land at a real Martian location (Jezero crater, Gale crater, Olympus Mons, and more) and must keep four survival bars from running out over five sols: oxygen, food, radiation shielding, and energy. Each bar is restored through a short one-touch minigame. Players turn CO₂ into oxygen like NASA's MOXIE, sweep dust off solar panels, water a Veggie-style greenhouse, stack water and regolith into a radiation shield, and drive a rover to collect samples.

The game answers the challenge's core question directly: every decision affects survival. Energy is shared, so every task spends it, and players must choose what comes first while dust storms and solar flares, based on NASA data, push back. Earth's warnings can arrive late because of the real communication delay.

We designed it for zero learning curve: icons instead of text, one big button per screen, and real science given as a one-line reward after each action. Real NASA photos and sounds are always framed and labeled, so kids can tell what is real.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

ASTRONAUT MISSION TRAINER is a browser game (playable on phones in landscape and on desktop) where kids aged 7 to 12 command a fictional future crewed base on Mars. Each session is a landing at a real Martian location and lasts five sols. Four survival bars drop over time: oxygen, food, radiation shield, and energy. If any bar reaches zero, the crew evacuates.

HOW IT WORKS

Players walk between rooms and play short minigames, each based on real NASA technology or missions:

- Oxygen factory: feed CO₂ into a machine that works like MOXIE on Perseverance.

- Solar panels: go outside through the airlock and sweep away Martian dust, which ended Opportunity's mission.

- Greenhouse: water plants like the Veggie experiment on the International Space Station.

- Shield wall: fill gaps with water and regolith blocks to stop radiation.

- Rover expedition: drive around soft sand (like the sand that trapped Spirit) and seal samples in tubes like Perseverance does.

Energy is the shared currency: every task except the panels spends it, so players must prioritize. Events based on real history (solar storms in 2003, 2017, and 2024, the 2018 global dust storm, InSight's dusty panels) arrive as warnings from Earth, sometimes late because of the real communication delay. In a crisis vote, kids choose a response and then see a real NASA image showing why it was right or wrong. Five locations (Jezero, Gale, Olympus Mons, the North Pole, Valles Marineris) get harder for real scientific reasons, with stars to unlock and replay.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

The challenge asks kids to understand that every decision affects survival. We make that the core loop instead of a lesson: there is never enough energy for everything. Science appears after each action as a one-line reward, never as a wall of text, so kids learn by playing. The game is bilingual (Spanish and English) so it reaches more children in Latin America.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

- Zero learning curve: icons, color, and animation instead of instructions; one large button per screen.

- Real NASA photos are always shown inside a window, monitor, or tablet and labeled as real, so kids can tell real images from game art. Photos taken from orbit are labeled as orbital.

- The soundtrack is NASA data sonifications (the galactic center and the Pillars of Creation), and the sound effects are real NASA recordings: the Artemis I launch, Apollo Quindar tones, and an InSight seismometer sound.

- An in-game Sources screen credits every fact and image.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

TypeScript, Phaser 3, Vite, Vitest, ESLint, and Prettier, deployed on Vercel. The game logic is pure TypeScript with no Phaser imports and is covered by unit tests, so it could move to a multiplayer server later. Game content (locations and events) lives in editable JSON files.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Accuracy (no text implies anything landed where it did not, and every fact is checked against a NASA source), touch targets sized for small hands, short sessions of about 5 minutes, and accessibility for kids who do not read fluently yet.

USE OF SI TOOLS

The pixel-art backgrounds, characters, and sprites were generated with SI image tools (ChatGPT and Gemini) and then edited by the team. We used SI coding assistants for coding, debugging, writing, and Spanish/English translation; every fact was checked by hand against the NASA sources listed below. All real NASA photos and sounds are unmodified apart from cropping, resizing, and trimming, and are credited on the in-game Sources screen. No NASA logos or branding were generated or modified.
